title: the GitHub data layer and the review surface, answered by the core rather than by the machine the app is on
asserts: a core that advertises `github` answers the whole PR surface itself, reads and writes: the folder's open PRs with the triage question and the order already applied, the search that reaches past the page cap, a branch's PR, a checkout's repo identity, one PR's conversation, that conversation merged into the chronology it is read in, a PR's net diff, a red build parsed into folds and lines, and the viewer's own cross-repo queue — plus opening a PR, commenting on one and re-running its build. They are HTTP because each one is a question somebody asks once and leaves, and every one of them used to be a `gh` call inside the desktop app, which is why a phone had no PR view at all. The decisions are made HERE and not in a client on purpose: 'is this PR waiting on me' is four rules with a priority between them, and 'which of these two comments came first' has three tie-breaks in it, and two clients that implemented either separately would eventually disagree about the same PR. The three writes are POSTs and not GETs, because each has a side effect on GitHub and a core that answered them on GET would be one a browser could fire by prefetching a link. The review surface is the other write half and goes over the wire, because a refresh is a whole model turn: held open as a request it would block the socket carrying every attached session's bytes, and answered as a frame it arrives when it is done. A staged comment is answered with the WHOLE list rather than with itself, because two surfaces stage comments against one session. The failures are as load-bearing as the answers: a read with no `cwd` is a 400 rather than a question about no repository, a PR `gh` cannot reach is a 502 rather than a 404 — a client told 'not found' would cache a PR out of existence — and a green PR's Actions log is a 200 with no sections rather than an error, because having no failing build is an answer.

steps.note: one call for the page, one for the viewer, one GraphQL for every PR's unresolved threads — and never one per folder, because fork+exec is a quarter of a second on the machine this was measured on. The rollup is a judgement rather than a count: two checks, one green and one red, is a red PR with `passedCount` 1. `unresolvedComments` is merged in afterwards because the list call cannot see thread resolution at all

the triage answer, in the order the pinned group is drawn: your own red PR outranks somebody else's review request, and #7 is in the list at all only because the viewer's review was requested on it. The label travels with the reason so no client keeps its own table of these four strings
the other order the list is shown in. GitHub numbers PRs at creation, so descending number IS descending submit date and there is no second field to fetch
a PR list with no folder is a question about no repository, so it is refused rather than answered for whatever directory the daemon happens to be standing in

the whole Conversation tab out of one GraphQL call, scoped by the owner/name lifted from the PR's own url so there is no extra `gh repo view`. An empty reaction bucket is not a reaction anybody left, so it is not in the list

three lists become one chronology, and the review carries the thread it started with BOTH turns in it. PRR_2 is not here: GitHub writes a bare COMMENTED review for every inline reply, and with no body, no reactions and no thread of its own it would draw as a card that says nothing while the reply it records is already on screen inside RT_1. The reply target is the thread's FIRST comment, because GitHub's replies API 422s on a reply to a reply

a red build read the way the Actions web UI reads it rather than as a 20k-character dump. Only the failing run's id is here because only its check failed. The error line is reachable without opening a fold, an unterminated `##[group]` is closed at the step boundary, and the ANSI is split into attributed spans with the raw SGR code kept — which red a client draws is its own business and depends on its theme
a 502 and not a 404. The route exists and the PR probably does; what failed is the hop to GitHub, and a client told 'not found' would cache a PR out of existence

the half of a folder's PRs the page cap hides. A list call answers the newest N and nothing else, so reaching an older PR — one of your own, or one an entered query matches — is a second, repo-scoped call whose result the caller unions in. The search is the caller's qualifiers verbatim: this core does not guess what `author:@me` was meant to mean
a search with no qualifiers is the list route with extra steps, and answering it would make the two indistinguishable to a caller that forgot the parameter
the single-branch lookup, which is a different `gh` call from the page: a session header asks about ONE branch and the list may not contain it

the stub answers every `--head` the same way, so this asserts only that the route is the lookup and not the page. A branch with no PR is a 200 with `pr: null` — not a 404 — because 'this branch has no PR' is an answer the header draws, and both a hit and a miss are cached by the caller

a checkout's repo identity. This is what maps a cross-repo queue row — which knows a repo and not a path — back onto a local checkout, so a row in a repo you have open gets the full detail pane instead of only 'open on GitHub'

a PR's net diff in the same per-file shape the working tree answers with, so one panel draws both. Not `--patch`: that emits a mailbox patch SERIES, one per commit, and a file touched in three commits parses into three same-path entries with per-commit rather than net counts. A rename is ONE entry at its new path carrying the old one, because `gh pr diff` emits `-M` similarity headers and a parser that read them as a delete and an add would draw a file twice. Sorted by path, which is where the moved README lands
a checkout `gh` cannot answer for. A 502 and not a 404 or an empty diff: an empty diff is a claim that the PR changed nothing, and a client shown one would draw a PR out of existence

the queue the folder list cannot answer: every open PR you wrote and every one that asked for your review, across repos you may have no clone of, out of ONE GraphQL call carrying both searches as aliases. The rows come back in the same shape the folder list produces — rollup, review decision, unresolved threads — so nothing needs a follow-up fetch. Authorship wins when both searches return the same PR, so each appears once. The attention reason is decided here for the same reason `needsYou` is; a review request is a reason in itself, because the search has already answered a question the PR payload cannot

a POST and not a GET: this has a side effect on GitHub, and a core that answered it on GET would be one a browser could fire by prefetching a link. The branch is NOT pushed here — the caller pushes first, because a core that pushed a branch as a side effect of a different verb would be one nobody could predict
a PR with no title is refused rather than opened with an empty one, which is a thing somebody then has to go and fix on github.com
the top-level comment

and the inline reply, on the same route: the composer is one box, and which of the two it posts is whether a thread is open under it. `replyTo` is the REST id of the thread's FIRST comment, because GitHub 422s a reply to a reply
an empty comment is a comment somebody has to delete
re-running the red half of a build. The run ids come from the PR's own checks, deduped, because several failing jobs usually belong to one Actions run and re-running it twice is two builds
a checkout with no runs behind it. A 502 carrying gh's own sentence, not a silent success: a button that reports 'done' having done nothing is worse than one that says why
the review surface is per session, and it reviews that session's own working tree — which is why this one starts in the dirty git checkout
a read, which costs nothing and is answered inline
absent rather than an empty result: 'nothing has reviewed this' is a different thing from 'a pass found nothing', and a client draws two different panels from them
a selection dragged upwards arrives backwards. That is a selection, not a mistake

answered with the WHOLE list rather than with the comment, because two surfaces stage comments against one session and a client patching its own copy would drift from the set the composer reads. The range is normalised and the body trimmed
refused rather than defaulted: a comment on the wrong side of a hunk hangs off a line the author never wrote
and the same set over HTTP, because the phone console reads it that way
a whole model turn. Off the connection's own task, which is the point of the frame: the socket it arrived on is carrying every attached session's pty bytes

the stand-in agent is not a `-p` JSON emitter, so the pass concludes that it could not read the CLI's output. That is the honest verdict and it is cached like any other: 'the last pass failed, and this is why' is what the panel shows, and losing it would make a failed review look like a review nobody ever ran
and the read again, which is the half of the round trip that proves it was stored
one cached pass, one row, reachable both ways
no comment id is the whole set: unstaging one comment and discarding the review you were composing are the same operation at two scopes
a miss is reported rather than swallowed: the client was holding a comment this core does not have
a session this core has never heard of, which is a different failure from a session with no review and reads as one
